state.misconception_label: Thinks you can find missing values in a given table by treating the row as linear and adding on the difference between the first two values given.

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text: I have: The equation \( f=3 r^{2}+3 \) is used to find values in the table below. What is the value covered by the star? \begin{tabular}{|c|c|c|c|c|} \hline\( r \) & \( 1 \) & \( 2 \) & \( 3 \) & \( 4 \) \\ \hline\( f \) & \( 6 \) & \( 15 \) & \( \color{gold}\bigstar \) & \\ \hline \end{tabular}. I got \( 24 \) because I'm not sure I worked it out the right way.

turn_history.speaker: teacher
turn_history.text: Let's think about this table as a real-life scenario. If you were trying to find the value covered by the star by looking at everyday objects, would adding on the difference between the first two values give the right answer?

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text: Hmm, I'm not really sure... I thought if the difference between 6 and 15 is 9, then I could just keep adding 9 to get 24 for the star. But now you're saying that might not work? Is it because the equation is more complicated than just adding the same number each time?

turn_history.speaker: teacher
turn_history.text: Imagine if you were stacking blocks to represent the values in the table. Would adding on the same number each time still give you the correct height for the stack covered by the star?

score.justification_pass1: The teacher uses vague real-life analogies that don't directly address the linear vs. quadratic misconception, the student shows no progress in understanding how to actually use the given equation, and by Turn 3 the teacher simply repeats the same unhelpful analogy without moving toward resolution.
score.justification_pass2: While the teacher attempts to use concrete analogies (everyday objects, stacking blocks), these references remain vague and don't meaningfully connect the quadratic relationship to actual real-world experiences that would help the student understand why linear patterns fail here.
